citeAs: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Burns, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt (2021). Measuring Mathematical Problem Solving With the MATH Dataset. NeurIPS 2021 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks.
creator: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Burns, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt (UC Berkeley, UChicago)
description: MATH is a dataset of 12,500 challenging competition mathematics problems (7,500 training and 5,000 test) sourced from high school math competitions including the AMC 10, AMC 12, and AIME. Each problem includes a full step-by-step solution written in LaTeX and natural language, a final boxed answer, a difficulty level from 1 to 5, and spans seven subjects: Prealgebra, Algebra, Number Theory, Counting and Probability, Geometry, Intermediate Algebra, and Precalculus.
name: MATH
rai:annotatorDemographics: Human evaluators (not annotators for labeling) were six university students studying computer science; four were authors on the paper, and two were friends or acquaintances of the authors. All participants gave consent. The problems themselves were created by the competition mathematics community (Mathematical Association of America).
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Problems and step-by-step solutions were created by the competition mathematics community (Mathematical Association of America) as part of official math competitions. Difficulty levels (1–5) follow the AoPS (Art of Problem Solving) difficulty scale. Final answers are wrapped with the \boxed{} LaTeX command to enable automatic evaluation.
rai:dataCollection: Problems were collected from mathematics competitions including the AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME, and more. Many problems were collected from aops.com/community/c3158_usa_contests. These competitions span decades and assess the mathematical problem-solving ability of the best young mathematical talent in the United States.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Competition mathematics problems from AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME, and other contests, sourced from aops.com. Problems are formatted in LaTeX and the Asymptote vector graphics language, with step-by-step solutions and final boxed answers.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is explicitly not intended to train models that help students cheat on mathematics exams. Human evaluation was limited to six participants (all university students studying computer science, four of whom are paper authors), so human-level performance estimates are rough. The dataset covers competition mathematics and may not represent all aspects of mathematical reasoning.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Problems and solutions are consistently formatted using LaTeX and the Asymptote vector graphics language. Final boxed answers follow consistent formatting rules: probabilities expressed as simplified fractions; matrix entry fractions encoded with x/y; other fractions encoded with \frac{x}{y}; coefficients encoded without multiplication symbol; expressions with multiple variables in alphabetical order; polynomials in decreasing degree order. Equivalent representations (e.g., \frac{x}{y} and \dfrac{x}{y}, \left( and (, 0.5 and 1/2) are treated as equivalent. Units may be included or omitted; spaces are ignored.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors note that even 40% accuracy for a machine learning model on MATH would be impressive but would have ramifications for cheating on homework. The dataset is intended to help the research community better forecast reasoning capabilities and drive algorithmic advancements in mathematical problem solving. The dataset is not sold and is likely to have no effect on the value of the original competition problems.
rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking mathematical problem-solving ability of machine learning models; training models to generate step-by-step answer derivations and explanations; forecasting reasoning capabilities of ML systems. The authors explicitly state they do not intend for the dataset to train models that help students cheat on mathematics exams.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: None. The dataset consists entirely of mathematics competition problems and solutions with no personal or sensitive information.
